parole.significato: a village
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish aldea and/or Portuguese aldeia.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of mass, varying by time, location, and substance but generally around 11.5 kilograms.
parole.testo: From Spanish and Portuguese arroba, from Old Spanish arroua and Old Galician-Portuguese arrova, from Andalusian Arabic and Arabic اَلرُّبْع (ar-rubʕ, “one-fourth”) in reference to its making up one fourth of a quintal.

parole.significato: Two-stage.
parole.testo: From Spanish bietápico or Portuguese bietápico.

parole.significato: A cabin or hut for relaxing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish cabaña and Portuguese cabana, both from Late Latin capanna. Doublet of cabane and cabin.

parole.significato: Any of the relatively small crocodilians of the genus Caiman, within the family Alligatoridae.
parole.testo: From Spanish caimán or Portuguese caimão, from Kari'na acayouman.

parole.significato: Any of four (previously two) species of parrot in the genus Pionites.
parole.testo: From Spanish caíque or Portuguese caíque.

parole.significato: bureau de change; currency exchange
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish or Portuguese cambio.

parole.significato: A field or plain in a Spanish- or Portuguese-speaking area.
parole.testo: From Spanish campo and/or Portuguese campo. Doublet of camp and campus.

parole.significato: A large semi-aquatic South American rodent of the genus Hydrochoerus.
parole.testo: From Spanish capibara, from Portuguese capivara, from Old Tupi kapi'iûara (literally “grass eater”).

parole.significato: Any of several South American and Central American birds of prey in the subfamily Caracarinae.
parole.testo: From Spanish caracara or Portuguese carcará, from Tupian, probably imitative.

parole.significato: One of various large carnivals held before the beginning of Lent, especially in Latin America.
parole.testo: From Spanish carnaval, Portuguese carnaval. Doublet of carnival.

parole.significato: The bedbug (Cimex lectularius).
parole.testo: From Spanish chinche (“bedbug”) or Portuguese chinche, from Latin cimex (“bedbug”). Doublet of cimex.

parole.significato: A violent squall with thunder and lightning, encountered during the rainy season along the Pacific coast of Central Ame…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish chubasco (“downpour”), from Portuguese chuva (“rain”), from Latin pluvia (“rain”).

parole.significato: Any of several omnivorous mammals, of the genus Nasua, that live in the range from the southern United States to northe…
parole.testo: From Spanish coatí, from Portuguese quati, coati, from Old Tupi kua'ti, from cua (“belt”) + tim (“nose”).

parole.significato: A contrabandist in Spain, Portugal, or Latin America.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Spanish contrabandista and Unadapted borrowing from Portuguese contrabandista.

parole.significato: A member of a social class, in the 16th-century Spanish colonies, who were born in the colonies but had European lineag…
parole.testo: From Spanish criollo, originally from Portuguese crioulo. Doublet of Creole, Crioulo, and Krio.

parole.significato: A traditional short Spanish unit of length, usually about equal to 1.75 cm.
parole.testo: From Spanish and Portuguese dedo (“digit, finger”), from Old Spanish and Old Galician-Portuguese dedo, from Latin digitus, from Proto-Indo-European *deyǵ- (“to show, to point out”). Doublet of digit.

parole.significato: The act of marking off a boundary or setting a limit, notably by belligerents signing a treaty or ceasefire.
parole.testo: First recorded c.1752, from Spanish línea de demarcación and/or Portuguese linha de demarcação, the demarcation line laid down by the Pope on May 4, 1493, dividing the New World between Spain and Portugal on a line 100 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. Both derive from demarcar, from de- + mar

parole.significato: A small, mischievous humanoid creature in Iberian (Spanish/Portuguese), Latin American, and Philippine folklore/mytholo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish duende and (especially in reference to Portuguese or Brazilian folklore) Portuguese duende. Doublet of duwende.

parole.significato: A purplish-blue color.
parole.testo: 16th century (as indico, modern spelling from the 17th century), Spanish índigo, Portuguese endego (modern índigo), or Dutch (via Portuguese) indigo, all from Latin indicum (“indigo”), from Ancient Greek ἰνδικόν (indikón, “Indian dye”), from Ἰνδία (Indía). Doublet of Indic.

parole.significato: A member of one of various indigenous peoples in the Americas, Pacific, and East Asia formerly subject to Spain or Port…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish indio, Portuguese índio.

parole.significato: The daughter of a king in Spain or Portugal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish infanta, Portuguese infanta, feminine of infante.

parole.significato: Any son of the king of Spain or Portugal, sometimes except the eldest or heir apparent.
parole.testo: From Spanish infante and Portuguese infante, both from Latin īnfāntem (“child”). Doublet of infant. Cognate with infantry.

parole.significato: Spanish league, a traditional Spanish unit of distance equivalent to about 4.2 km.
parole.testo: From Spanish legua (“Spanish league”) and Portuguese légua (“Portuguese league”), from Late Latin leuga and leuca (“Gaulish league, distance of one hour's walking”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *lougā. Doublet of league.

parole.significato: One who exhibits ludopathy (problem gambling).
parole.testo: From ludo- + -path; a calque of Spanish ludópata or of Portuguese ludopata.

parole.significato: A drink made from manioc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish manicuera and Portuguese manicuera.

parole.significato: A small South American monkey (Mico melanurus, syn. Callithrix melanura), allied to the marmoset.
parole.testo: From Spanish or Portuguese mico.

parole.significato: The driver of a mototaxi.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mototaxista and Portuguese mototaxista.

parole.significato: An unrefined brown sugar with a strong flavour of molasses.
parole.testo: Corrupted from Spanish mascabado or Portuguese mascavado, from the verb mascavar, a corrupted form of menoscabar (“to despise”).

parole.significato: A rich, thick, Spanish stew consisting of meat and vegetables.
parole.testo: From Spanish olla or Portuguese olha, both from Latin olla (“pot, jar”).

parole.significato: Any of the large rodents of the genus Cuniculus (but see also its synonyms), native to Central America and South Americ…
parole.testo: Via Spanish paca and Portuguese paca, from Paraguayan Guarani paka.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about 20.8 cm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish palmo (“handspan”) and Portuguese palmo (“handspan”), both from Latin palmus. Doublet of palm, palma, and pam.

parole.significato: An American trick-taking card game of the all fours family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish and Portuguese Pedro, from Latin Petrus, from Ancient Greek Πέτρος (Pétros), from πέτρος (pétros, “stone, rock”). Doublet of Peter, Piers, Pietro, and Boutros.

parole.significato: A person or business that provides supplies, particularly food and beverages.
parole.testo: From Spanish proveedor or Portuguese provedor (“provider”), perhaps via Venetan. From Latin prōvideō (“to foresee”). Doublet of purveyor and proveditor.

parole.significato: Synonym of carat in historical Iberian contexts.
parole.testo: From Spanish and Portuguese quilate, from Arabic قِيرَاط (qīrāṭ, “carat”), from Ancient Greek κεράτιον (kerátion, “hornlet, carob seed”). Doublet of carat and ceratium.

parole.significato: A line which crosses successive meridians at a constant angle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish rumbo or Portuguese rumo, from Latin rhombus, from Ancient Greek ῥόμβος (rhómbos). Doublet of rhomb and rhombus.

parole.significato: A rectangular, hard, dry biscuit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish or Portuguese rosca (“a twist or roll of bread”)

parole.significato: The native people from the Santa Cruz area of California.
parole.testo: From Spanish and Portuguese Santa Cruz (“Holy Cross”), various places named in honor of the True Cross upon which Jesus was crucified. Doublet of Holy Cross and Saint Croix.

parole.significato: [I] speak.
parole.testo: From speak + -o, in imitation of Spanish hablo and Portuguese falo.

parole.significato: A South American omnivore, Eira barbara, allied to the grison, with a long thick tail.
parole.testo: Borrowed, via Spanish tayra or Portuguese taira, from Old Tupi eîrara. (Compare Portuguese irara, Spanish irará, eirá, connected to Paraguayan Guarani eíra (“honey”), a food the animal is fond of, whence also Portuguese papa-mel, another vernacular name.)

parole.significato: Synonym of estado, Spanish toise or fathom, a traditional unit of length, equivalent to about 1.67 m.
parole.testo: From Spanish and Portuguese toesa, from French toise. Doublet of toise.

parole.significato: A member of a Latin American gender role, variously construed as a cross-dressing man, a third gender or a trans woman.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish travesti and Portuguese travesti, themselves both from French travesti. Doublet of travesty.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about 83.7 cm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish and Portuguese vara (“rod”), from Latin vāra (“fork”).

parole.significato: A warning on a navigational chart indicating a reef or other hazard which has been reported but which has not been conf…
parole.testo: From Spanish vigía (“lookout; reef”), from Portuguese vigia, ultimately from Latin vigilare.

parole.significato: The most virulent form of yellow fever.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish vómito and Portuguese vómito, from Latin vomitus.
